youtube.title: Why 97% of Day Traders Lose Money (The Data)
youtube.description:
Why do 97% of day traders lose money? We go through the real data: a study of everyone who day traded futures in Brazil for 300+ days, 15 years of day trading records from Taiwan, and 60,000+ U.S. brokerage households, plus what changed in 2026 when the $25,000 pattern day trader minimum went away.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:24 The 300-day study
1:16 It's not just Brazil
1:57 Trading more, earning less
2:34 Why the math is brutal
3:41 The rule that changed
4:40 What wins instead
5:26 Recap

Numbers in this video
• 97% of people who started day trading Brazilian equity futures in 2013–2015 and kept going for at least 300 days lost money; only 0.4% earned more than a bank teller's starting pay (about US$54/day); the top trader earned about US$310/day with very high risk; no evidence of learning (Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti, "Day Trading for a Living?", FGV EESP working paper)
• Taiwan, 1992–2006: about 450,000 day traders in an average year; about 5% profitable in a given year; less than 1% predictably profitable after fees; more than 75% quit within two years; day traders as a group lost money after fees in every one of the 15 years (Barber, Lee, Liu & Odean, Journal of Financial Markets 2014; Barber, Lee, Liu, Odean & Zhang, "Do Day Traders Rationally Learn About Their Ability?")
• 60,000+ U.S. households at a discount broker, 1991–1996: market (value-weighted index) 17.1% a year; average household 15.3% net; the 20% who traded most 10.0% net (Barber & Odean, "Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth", Journal of Finance 2000)
• In 2026 the SEC approved FINRA Rule 4210 changes that eliminate the pattern day trader rules, including the $25,000 minimum; brokers began applying them in June 2026 and a $2,000 margin minimum still applies (FINRA/SEC; E*TRADE client notice, June 2026). Check your own broker's rules.
• India, FY2025-26: 87.7% of individual equity derivatives (F&O) traders made net losses (SEBI study, August 2026)
• Short-term gains (assets held one year or less) are taxed at ordinary income rates in the U.S. (IRS Topic 409)
• The $10.02/$10.00 spread and the 15-year bar heights are illustrations.
